extraction.name: HELVIPAD : A Real-World Dataset for Omnidirectional Stereo Depth Estimation
extraction.description: HELVIPAD is a comprehensive real-world dataset for stereo depth estimation from 360° images. It consists of 29 video sequences captured in dynamic indoor and outdoor scenes across a university campus, under diverse weather and lighting conditions. Data were collected using a custom-built rig equipped with two omnidirectional cameras in a vertical arrangement, which prevents occlusion, and paired with a synchronized LiDAR sensor to provide high-quality depth measurements. Applying depth completion, the training data is augmented with a significantly increased label density. With a total of 39,553 labeled frames, HELVIPAD serves as a foundational resource for developing and benchmarking omnidirectional depth estimation models capable of navigating in human environments.
extraction.creator: Mehdi Zayene, Jannik Endres, Albias Havolli, Charles Corbière, Salim Cherkaoui, Alexandre Kontouli, Alexandre Alahi
extraction.citeAs: Mehdi Zayene, Jannik Endres, Albias Havolli, Charles Corbière, Salim Cherkaoui, Alexandre Kontouli, Alexandre Alahi. HELVIPAD : A Real-World Dataset for Omnidirectional Stereo Depth Estimation. arXiv:2411.18335v2 [cs.CV], 25 Mar 2025.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Data was collected across distinct scenes, encompassing indoor (e.g., corridors, halls) and outdoor (e.g., squares, external parking, footpaths) settings in various lighting conditions on a university campus. The rig features two Ricoh Theta V 360° cameras in a top-bottom setup with a 19.1 cm baseline, capturing equirectangular images at 30 fps, paired with an Ouster OS1-64 LiDAR sensor with a vertical field of view of 42.4°, operating at 10 fps, and mounted 45.0 cm below the bottom camera. A central processor manages data capture and ensures device synchronization. In total, 29 video sequences were collected. The dataset includes 26 video sequences captured between December 2023 and February 2024, recorded at a frame rate of 10 Hz. Each sequence is synchronized with its corresponding LiDAR point clouds, which are projected on frames to obtain depth maps, and subsequently disparity maps. Top images, bottom images, depth maps, and disparity maps are then cropped to remove unnecessary borders and downsized from a width of 1024 pixels to 512 to enable more efficient training. The sequences span a diverse array of settings and conditions, including recordings taken at various times of the day, from early morning to night, under a variety of weather conditions, including cloudy and sunny skies. These recordings were made in multiple indoor and outdoor locations, from pedestrian squares and footpaths to corridors and parking areas. The dynamic nature of the recorded scenes is emphasized by the presence of pedestrians, with an average of 13.33 pedestrians in indoor sequences and 17.65 pedestrians in outdoor sequences.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Given the sparse nature of LiDAR point clouds compared to high-resolution camera images, ground-truth depth labels cover only a fraction of the total pixels.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data was collected using a custom-built rig equipped with two Ricoh Theta V 360° cameras in a top-bottom setup and an Ouster OS1-64 LiDAR sensor. The cameras capture images in 4K/UHD equirectangular format at 30 fps with an initial resolution of 3840 × 1920 pixels. The LiDAR sensor operates at 10 fps with 64 beams and a vertical field of view of 42.4°. A central processor manages data capture and ensures device synchronization.
extraction.rai:dataImputationProtocol: To address the sparse nature of LiDAR point clouds, a fully automated depth completion pipeline tailored for 360° images was developed. This approach interpolates depth on spherical grid points by using temporally aggregated point clouds and applies a filtering process to exclude points with high uncertainty or lacking nearby measurements, ensuring minimal error before mapping the remaining points. Temporal aggregation involves fusing the current frame's point cloud with those from the four preceding and four succeeding frames. Interpolation estimates depth for a query point (theta_q, phi_q) within the LiDAR’s field of view through a weighted average of its k-nearest neighbors. Filtering ensures high-quality depth labels by excluding query points exceeding either an uncertainty criterion (relative weighted variance of interpolated depth values) or an out-of-distribution threshold (average distance to k-nearest neighbors). The pipeline significantly increases the ratio of labeled pixels from 12% to 61% while maintaining very low error rates.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Top images, bottom images, depth maps, and disparity maps are cropped to remove unnecessary borders and downsized from a width of 1024 pixels to 512 to enable more efficient training.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The main challenge in processing raw data is to ensure a robust and accurate projection of the LiDAR point clouds on the 360° camera images. The algorithm involves selecting key 3D points in the point cloud obtained by LiDAR scans on a 19x19 chessboard, focusing on corners and edge midpoints to obtain their coordinates. Corresponding image pixel positions are selected in the equirectangular bottom image. Initial rotation and translation transformations are applied to make the camera lens the coordinate system’s center, ensuring alignment with the camera’s viewpoint. The transformed points are then converted into spherical coordinates and projected onto the equirectangular plane. The core step is the optimization of rotation and translation parameters by minimizing the error between projected points and their corresponding location on the equirectangular images. These optimized parameters compose the best-fit transformation to align LiDAR point clouds on the bottom equirectangular images. The average pixel error for alignment accuracy is 1.7 pixels, remaining low at 8.0 pixels in visually challenging areas. Spherical disparity is then obtained from depth values.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Accurate depth and disparity labels are generated by projecting 3D point clouds from a synchronized LiDAR sensor onto equirectangular images. The LiDAR-to-image mapping optimization algorithm involves selecting LiDAR points and their corresponding image points, transforming LiDAR points to camera coordinates, converting them to spherical coordinates, and projecting them to equirectangular coordinates. The total error between projected points and image points is minimized using BFGS to optimize rotation and translation parameters. Spherical disparity is then calculated from depth values using a specific equation involving polar angle, depth, and camera baseline.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: To assess alignment accuracy, the pixel error was calculated by measuring Euclidean distances between 200 randomly selected LiDAR points and their image positions, resulting in an average error of 1.7 pixels. When selecting the same number of points from visually challenging areas (e.g., object edges), the error remained relatively low at 8.0 pixels, confirming calibration quality. Occlusions were not explicitly handled, as the small LiDAR-camera baseline minimizes their impact. For depth completion, the pipeline was validated by splitting each LiDAR point cloud into training and test sets and computing depth estimation metrics on the test set. This process significantly increased the ratio of labeled pixels from 12% to 61% while maintaining very low error rates. The evaluation metrics for depth completion include Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), mean absolute relative error (MARE), Inlier Ratio (IR), and Actual Ratio of Interpolated Points (ARIP).
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The dataset captures human pedestrian activity, with an average of 13.33 pedestrians in indoor sequences and 17.65 pedestrians in outdoor sequences. No specific sensitive human attributes (e.g., gender, socio-economic status, geography, language, age, culture, experience) are explicitly mentioned as collected or extracted.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: Mobile robots are increasingly used in real-world applications such as autonomous driving, healthcare, or agriculture, where accurate 3D representations of dynamic human environments are crucial for navigation and interaction. This dataset aims to help build these representations by estimating the distance of surrounding objects from the robot’s viewpoint. The work hopes to encourage further research into omnidirectional stereo matching, especially for real-time applications.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The temporal aggregation approach for depth completion is limited for fast-moving objects like cars. The evaluation of depth completion metrics over points with low distances to its neighbors, which are easier to estimate, may reflect lower bounds on actual errors due to this distribution shift. The dataset was collected on a university campus, which might introduce biases related to the specific environment and demographics present there.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset is limited for fast-moving objects like cars due to the temporal aggregation approach used in depth completion. The evaluation of depth completion metrics may reflect lower bounds on actual errors due to a distribution shift. The dataset was collected on a university campus, which might limit its generalization to other environments. The sparsity of LiDAR point clouds means ground-truth depth labels cover only a fraction of the total pixels. The depth completion method does not provide labels for pixels at object boundaries, as it is challenging to ascertain their precise locations based on depth data alone. The dataset lacks odometry information, which could be useful for certain temporal aggregation methods. The dataset is an ideal testbed for assessing the robustness of depth estimation methods to diverse lighting conditions and depth ranges.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, Testing, Validation, Fine Tuning. The dataset serves as a foundational resource for developing and benchmarking omnidirectional depth estimation models capable of navigating in human environments. It is an ideal testbed for assessing the robustness of depth estimation methods to diverse lighting conditions and depth ranges.
